analysis.one_liner: Extends the Minuteman III missile to 2040 and halts spending on a new ICBM.
analysis.headline: The bill to pause a new intercontinental ballistic missile program estimated at $264 billion over its life was referred to two House committees and never received a markup, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred defense funds from fiscal years 2022 through 2031 from being spent on the ground-based strategic deterrent program — the Air Force's new intercontinental ballistic missile, projected at $93 billion to $96 billion to buy and about $264 billion over its lifetime — and on the $12 billion W87-1 warhead modification for it [S2] [S3]. Instead, it directed the Pentagon to extend the life of the existing Minuteman III missiles to 2040, an option the Congressional Budget Office projected would cost about $37 billion less through 2036 than building the new missile [S2] [S3]. The bill's findings argue the savings are real and that the land-based missile leg of the nuclear force raises the risk of an accidental nuclear war that submarine-based missiles do not [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would avoid tens of billions of dollars in near-term spending and a projected $264 billion lifetime cost for the new missile program; the bill's findings also argue the public gains from reducing the risk of an accidental nuclear launch by keeping the existing, recall-able posture rather than replacing it [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers footing the nuclear modernization bill

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any funds for fiscal years 2022 through 2031 from being obligated or expended on the ground-based strategic deterrent program or the W87-1 warhead modification, and blocks reprogramming of unobligated warhead funds.

Directs a Minuteman III life-extension program to keep the existing missiles flying until 2040, which the Congressional Budget Office projected would cost $37 billion less through 2036 than the new missile program.
The findings cite a sole-source 2020 contract awarded to Northrop Grumman for the new missile, arguing the lack of competition could raise costs to taxpayers beyond projections.

The findings argue intercontinental ballistic missiles cannot be recalled and force leaders into minutes-long launch decisions, while submarine-based missiles provide an assured retaliatory capability without that risk, citing former defense officials William Perry, James Cartwright, and George Lee Butler.

analysis.who_pays: Northrop Grumman, which holds the sole-source development contract for the new missile, and the nuclear weapons industry — including the National Nuclear Security Administration's warhead modification and plutonium pit production work — would lose the program revenue the bill would pause.
analysis.who_pays_short: Northrop Grumman and nuclear weapons contractors

drawbacks.text: An Air Force general testified in 2019 that there was 'one more opportunity' to life-extend the Minuteman III, meaning betting on the existing missiles until 2040 carries real technical risk if the extension fails or costs more than expected.

Supporters of the new missile argue the land-based leg is needed to force an adversary to expend its own missiles in a first strike and that the triad's redundancy deters attack; the bill pauses rather than cancels the program, deferring but not eliminating the eventual replacement decision and its cost.
Extending a 1970s-design missile to 2040 requires new command-and-control and missile-defense-resilience technologies, and the bill does not estimate the cost of that life-extension work itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is straightforward: keep a proven missile flying for roughly $37 billion less through 2036, against the risk that the life extension proves harder or costlier than projected and that the replacement decision merely gets pushed to a later Congress at higher eventual cost. The safety argument in its findings — that recall-able, sea-based forces make an accidental land-based launch unnecessary — is a serious one, but it is a judgment about nuclear strategy on which senior military officials have disagreed, preferring the new missile.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Armed Services and Appropriations committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and the Congress ended in January 2023 with no markup, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. John Garamendi introduced the bill on June 30, 2021, joined by nine Democratic cosponsors, all from the House.
The House referred it to the Committee on Armed Services and, in addition, to the Committee on Appropriations; that referral was the only action the bill ever received.
No committee markup, hearing action, vote, or floor consideration followed, and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with the bill still pending in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Northrop Grumman, which holds the sole-source development contract for the new missile, and the wider nuclear weapons industrial base kept the program and its projected $93 billion to $264 billion in spending on track, since nothing interrupted the Pentagon's modernization plans.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Northrop Grumman and nuclear weapons contractors

for.name: Rep. John Garamendi
for.role: Sponsor, House Armed Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor the day it was introduced.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote, no report.

against.name: House Appropriations Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; because the bill never reached a vote, there is no roll call to show how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: Northrop Grumman won a sole-source contract in September 2020 for the new missile's development; the bill would have cut off its funding for a decade. Its gain depends on taxpayer spending the bill's own findings say could exceed projections because of the lack of competition.

industries.industry: Nuclear weapons complex (National Nuclear Security Administration warhead and plutonium pit work)
industries.note: The bill would have frozen the $12 billion W87-1 warhead modification and blocked reprogramming of unobligated warhead funds, hitting the government-run and contractor-run weapons production enterprise built around the new missile.
Directing a Minuteman III life-extension program to 2040 shifts money from building a new missile to maintaining and upgrading the existing one, work performed under existing sustainment contracts.
